rows.topic: The family version of the 30 plants page, replacing the 2026-05 adult gut-science article (rewrite: the file is written fresh, legacy: true goes, slug stays). The guideline in one honest paragraph: the American Gut Project found that adults who ate 30 or more plant types a week had a more diverse gut microbiome (McDonald 2018); an observation in adults, never a promise for a child (brand-stats-and-claims). Then the part a family uses: what a plant is (fruit, groente, peulvruchten, volkoren granen, noten, zaden, kruiden, specerijen), why variety beats quantity, how one week of family meals adds up (a pasta night is 4 or 5 plants), how to count as a household without it becoming a project, the tasting count as the child's side of the same game, the groceries moment (what has the family not had in three weeks). Sections: what the 30 means, what counts (short, links the live cluster /nl/leer/plant-diversity/what-counts-as-a-plant), counting as a family (short, announces the planned cluster with one sentence copied verbatim into that row's pillar_mention), the first week, what backfires (the count as a chore, a child's plate as a score, comparing siblings). No microbiome claim for children, no 'gezond' as judgment.

rows.topic: The psychology behind a child who refuses food, in parent words and without a diagnosis: autonomy at 2 to 3 (no is the first power a child has), control (the table is the one place a child decides what goes in), attention (a refused plate gets more of it than a finished one), the parent's own worry arriving at the table, fear of the new (neofobia in one line, link food-neophobia), the sensory side (texture, temperature, mixed foods) said plainly. Then what it means at the table: give the choice back in small ways (which of two vegetables, which plate), take the attention off the plate, eat together, one calm sentence and then let it be. What backfires (pressure, bribes, negotiating). The live page il-bambino-non-mangia covers the practical side and the red flags; this page is the why and links it in the first section. When to talk to the pediatra: one paragraph, no humour. Cites Dovey 2008 for the phase. rows.topic: The two-year dip as its own page: a child who ate everything and, around 2, eats much less or refuses whole meals. Why (growth slows after the first year and appetite follows; autonomy; neofobia starts), what a normal week looks like (some days almost nothing, some days a lot; count the week, not the meal), what helps at 2 (small portions, fixed meal moments, no milk or juice right before, eat together, the same food many times). The two searches parents add: 'non mangia da solo' (a 2-year-old who wants to be fed or refuses the spoon: normal, offer both, no fight) and 'non mangia a pezzi' (still on purées or refusing pieces: move to pieces one texture at a time, soft first, next to a safe food; if gagging or panic persists, the pediatra). What backfires. The forum question answered calmly: most 2-year-olds who stop eating start again, the phase passes for most (Dovey 2008). When to talk to the pediatra (weight, fewer than about 20 foods, distress). Pillar: no announcement sentence exists; add the link sentence in the section 'Quando il bambino non mangia quasi niente'.

rows.topic: Two checklists on one page, each a real list a parent can tick tonight. Checklist 1, before you worry: 10 things to try for two weeks (fixed meal moments, small portions, one taste next to a safe food, eat together, no drinks or snacks in the hour before, no screens, reward the taste not the plate, the same food many times, count the week, one question after dinner). Checklist 2, take this to your doctor: 6 signs (losing weight or not growing, fewer than about 20 different foods, whole food groups missing, gagging or panic at new food, dropping accepted foods without replacing them, the worry is too big for you). Between them, one paragraph on what is normal at 2 to 6 (Dovey 2008) so a parent knows which list they are on. The search phrase in the title; the body never labels the child. No diagnosis; ARFID named once and referred out; referral word 'your doctor'. British spelling. elke dag strijd met peuter met eten
rows.topic: The table dynamic as its own page: why dinner turns into a fight (the parent decides the child must eat, the child discovers that no is a power, both dig in), the division that ends it (the parent decides what, when and where; the child decides whether and how much; in plain words, no author name), how a dinner without a fight goes in practice (one sentence about the taste, then talk about the day; the plate stays 20 minutes and goes; no cooking twice; no negotiating). The questions in the search: 'peuter weigert te eten' (the week counts, not the meal), 'wil niet aan tafel eten' (a chair with feet on a step, short meals, the child comes when dinner starts and may leave when done), 'zonder eten naar bed' (a toddler who skips dinner usually catches up tomorrow; no punishment, no second dinner, the same calm breakfast; if it happens every night, look at the day: drinks, snacks, sleep), 'elke dag strijd' (two weeks of the tasting count instead of the plate, link). What backfires. When to ask the consultatiebureau (weight, distress, fewer than about 20 foods). Cites Cooke 2011 for rewarding the taste; no health claim. The pillar_mention sentence is not an announcement: replace it with a sentence that keeps its meaning and links the article.
rows.pillar_mention: Wat helpt: vaste eetmomenten, kleine porties, weinig drinken en snacks vlak voor het eten, en geen strijd.
